claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a fine-grained fcc matrix in its starting state.
Post-processing heat treatment can increase grain size while maintaining the fcc phase.
The proposed heat treatment can modify grain-boundary character without altering other microstructural constituents.
Grain coarsening increases the fast diffusion pathways available to reactive species.
Grain boundaries act as fast diffusion pathways for reactive species in this alloy.
Grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for continuous oxide scales or suboxide phases.
Coarsened grain boundaries permit deeper and more uniform ingress of oxygen or reducing-environment species.
Deeper reactive-species ingress produces thicker and more interconnected oxide scales or boundary depletion zones.
Boundary oxidation or depletion promotes intergranular embrittlement.
Intergranular degradation creates stress concentrations that can cause catastrophic failure under thermal cycling or applied load.
In oxidizing environments, coarse-grained samples will develop thicker and more networked oxide scales than as-built fine-grained samples.
In reducing environments, coarse-grained samples will develop more pronounced grain-boundary voids than as-built fine-grained samples.
Coarse-grained samples will initiate intergranular cracking earlier than as-built fine-grained samples.
Coarse-grained samples will have lower mechanical strength and fail catastrophically earlier than as-built fine-grained samples.
The proposed mechanism applies from 750 to 900 °C for exposures up to 100 hours in oxidizing or reducing atmospheres when phase transformations do not interfere.
Precipitate formation or other unintended microstructural changes during heat treatment could confound attribution of degradation to grain-boundary coarsening.
Absence of a statistically significant increase in degradation, intergranular cracking, or earlier failure in coarse-grained samples would falsify the hypothesis.
